*Study note:* *Psalm 51*. The psalmist confesses his sinfulness to God and begs for forgiveness and a transformation of his inner character. According to the psalm superscription, David offered this prayer when Nathan confronted him with his sin following the king’s affair with Bathsheba (see 2 Sam 11-12). However, the final two verses of the psalm hardly fit this situation, for they assume the walls of Jerusalem have been destroyed and that the sacrificial system has been temporarily suspended. These verses are probably an addition to the psalm made during the period of exile following the fall of Jerusalem in 586 b.c. The exiles could relate to David’s experience, for they, like him, and had been forced to confront their sin. They appropriated David’s ancient prayer and applied it to their own circumstances.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “a psalm by David, when Nathan the prophet came to him when he had gone to Bathsheba.”

*Translator's note:* Or “according to.”

*Translator's note:* Or “according to.”

*Translator's note:* Traditionally “blot out my transgressions.” Because of the reference to washing and cleansing in the following verse, it is likely that the psalmist is comparing forgiveness to wiping an object clean (note the use of the verb מָחָה (makhah) in the sense of “wipe clean; dry” in {{2 Kings 21:13|2 Kgs 21:13}}; {{Proverbs 30:20|Prov 30:20}}; {{Isaiah 25:8|Isa 25:8}}). Another option is that the psalmist is comparing forgiveness to erasing or blotting out names from a register (see {{Exodus 32:32|Exod 32:32-33}}). In this case one might translate, “erase all record of my rebellious acts.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Thoroughly wash me from my wrongdoing.”

*Study note:* In vv. {{Psalm 51:1|1b-2}} the psalmist uses three different words to emphasize the multifaceted character and degree of his sin. Whatever one wants to call it (“rebellious acts,” “wrongdoing,” “sin”), he has done it and stands morally polluted in God’s sight. The same three words appear in {{Exodus 34:7|Exod 34:7}}, which emphasizes that God is willing to forgive sin in all of its many dimensions. In v. {{Psalm 51:2|2}} the psalmist compares forgiveness and restoration to physical cleansing. Perhaps he likens spiritual cleansing to the purification rites of priestly law.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “know.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and my sin [is] in front of me continually.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “only you,” as if the psalmist had sinned exclusively against God and no other. Since the Hebrew verb חָטָא (hataʾ, “to sin”) is used elsewhere of sinful acts against people (see BDB 306 s.v. 2.a) and David (the presumed author) certainly sinned when he murdered Uriah ({{2 Samuel 12:9|2 Sam 12:9}}), it is likely that the psalmist is overstating the case to suggest that the attack on Uriah was ultimately an attack on God himself. To clarify the point of the hyperbole, the translation uses “above all,” rather than the potentially confusing “only.”

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew term לְמַעַן (lemaʿan) normally indicates purpose (“in order that”), but here it introduces a logical consequence of the preceding statement. (Taking the clause as indicating purpose here would yield a theologically preposterous idea—the psalmist purposely sinned so that God’s justice might be vindicated!) For other examples of לְמַעַן indicating result, see {{2 Kings 22:17|2 Kgs 22:17}}; Jer 27:15; {{Amos 2:7|Amos 2:7}}, as well as *IBHS* 638-40 §38.3.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “when you speak.” In this context the psalmist refers to God’s word of condemnation against his sin delivered through Nathan (cf. {{2 Samuel 12:7|2 Sam 12:7-12}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “when you judge.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Look, in wrongdoing I was brought forth, and in sin my mother conceived me.” The prefixed verbal form in the second line is probably a preterite (without vav [ו] consecutive), stating a simple historical fact. The psalmist is not suggesting that he was conceived through an inappropriate sexual relationship (although the verse has sometimes been understood to mean that, or even that *all* sexual relationships are sinful). The psalmist’s point is that he has been a sinner from the very moment his personal existence began. By going back beyond the time of birth to the moment of conception, the psalmist makes his point more emphatically in the second line than in the first.

*Study note:* The juxtaposition of two occurrences of “*look*” in vv. {{Psalm 51:5|5-6}} draws attention to the sharp contrast between the sinful reality of the psalmist’s condition and the lofty ideal God has for him.

*Translator's note:* The perfect is used in a generalizing sense here.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “in the covered [places],” i.e., in the inner man.

*Study note:* *You want me to possess wisdom*. Here “wisdom” does not mean “intelligence” or “learning,” but refers to moral insight and skill.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “in the secret [place] wisdom you cause me to know.” The Hiphil verbal form is causative, while the imperfect is used in a modal sense to indicate God’s desire (note the parallel verb “desire”).

*Translator's note:* The imperfect verbal form is used here to express the psalmist’s wish or request.

*Study note:* “Hyssop” was a small plant (see {{1 Kings 4:33|1 Kgs 4:33}}) used to apply water or blood in purification rites (see {{Exodus 12:22|Exod 12:22}}; Lev 14:4-6, 49-52; {{Numbers 19:6|Num 19:6-18}}). The psalmist uses the language and imagery of such rites to describe spiritual cleansing through forgiveness.

*Translator's note:* After the preceding imperfect, the imperfect with vav (ו) conjunctive indicates result.

*Translator's note:* The imperfect verbal form is used here to express the psalmist’s wish or request.

*Study note:* *I will be whiter than snow*. Whiteness here symbolizes the moral purity resulting from forgiveness (see {{Isaiah 1:18|Isa 1:18}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “cause me to hear happiness and joy.” The language is metonymic: the effect of forgiveness (joy) has been substituted for its cause. The psalmist probably alludes here to an assuring word from God announcing that his sins are forgiven (a so-called oracle of forgiveness). The imperfect verbal form is used here to express the psalmist’s wish or request. The synonyms “happiness” and “joy” are joined together as a hendiadys to emphasize the degree of joy he anticipates.

*Study note:* *May the bones you crushed rejoice*. The psalmist compares his sinful condition to that of a person who has been physically battered and crushed. Within this metaphorical framework, his “bones” are the seat of his emotional strength.

*Translator's note:* In this context of petitionary prayer, the prefixed verbal form is understood as a jussive, expressing the psalmist’s wish or request.

*Study note:* In this context *Hide your face from my sins* means “Do not hold me accountable for my sins.”

*Translator's note:* See the note on the similar expression “wipe away my rebellious acts” in v. {{Psalm 51:1|1}}.

*Study note:* The *heart* is viewed here as the seat of the psalmist’s motives and moral character.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and a reliable spirit renew in my inner being.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “do not cast me away from before you.”

*Study note:* *Your holy Spirit*. The personal Spirit of God is mentioned frequently in the OT, but only here and in {{Isaiah 63:10|Isa 63:10-11}} is he called “your/his holy Spirit.”

*Study note:* *Do not take…away*. The psalmist expresses his fear that, due to his sin, God will take away the Holy Spirit from him. NT believers enjoy the permanent gift of the Holy Spirit and need not make such a request nor fear such a consequence. However, in the OT God’s Spirit empowered certain individuals for special tasks and only temporarily resided in them. For example, when God rejected Saul as king and chose David to replace him, the divine Spirit left Saul and came upon David ({{1 Samuel 16:13|1 Sam 16:13-14}}). An alternative understanding of this verse is that the term *Holy Spirit* is simply metaphorical for the Lord’s presence, but this is unlikely given the other use of the term in {{Isaiah 63:10|Isa 63:10}}, where the Holy Spirit is personal and distinct from God himself.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and [with] a willing spirit sustain me.” The psalmist asks that God make him the kind of person who willingly obeys the divine commandments. The imperfect verbal form is used here to express the psalmist’s wish or request.

*Translator's note:* The cohortative expresses the psalmist’s resolve. This may be a vow or promise. If forgiven, the psalmist will “repay” the Lord by declaring God’s mercy and motivating other sinners to repent.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “your ways.” The word “merciful” is added for clarification. God’s “ways” are sometimes his commands, but in this context, where the teaching of God’s ways motivates repentance (see the next line), it is more likely that God’s merciful and compassionate way of dealing with sinners is in view. Thanksgiving songs praising God for his deliverance typically focus on these divine attributes (see {{Psalm 34|Pss 34}}, {{Psalm 41|41}}, {{Psalm 116|116}}, {{Psalm 138|138}}).

*Translator's note:* Or “return,” i.e., in repentance.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “from bloodshed.” “Bloodshed” here stands by metonymy for the guilt which it produces.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “my tongue will shout for joy your righteousness.” Another option is to take the prefixed verbal form as a jussive, “may my tongue shout for joy.” However, the pattern in vv. {{Psalm 51:12|12-15}} appears to be prayer/request (see vv. {{Psalm 51:12|12}}, {{Psalm 51:14|14a}}, {{Psalm 51:15|15a}}) followed by promise/vow (see vv. {{Psalm 51:13|13}}, {{Psalm 51:14|14b}}, {{Psalm 51:15|15b}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “open my lips.” The imperfect verbal form is used here to express the psalmist’s wish or request.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and my mouth will declare your praise.”

*Translator's note:* Or “For.” The translation assumes the particle is asseverative (i.e., emphasizing: “certainly”). (Some translations that consider the particle asseverative leave it untranslated.) If taken as causal or explanatory (“for”, cf. NRSV), the verse would explain why the psalmist is pleading for forgiveness, rather than merely offering a sacrifice.

*Translator's note:* The translation assumes that the cohortative is used in a hypothetical manner in a formally unmarked conditional sentence, “You do not want a sacrifice, should I offer [it]” (cf. NEB). For other examples of cohortatives in the protasis (“if” clause) of a conditional sentence, see GKC 320 §108.*e*. (It should be noted, however, that *GKC* understands this particular verse in a different manner. See GKC 320 §108.*f*, where it is suggested that the cohortative is part of an apodosis with the protasis being suppressed.)

*Study note:* *You do not desire a burnt sacrifice*. The terminology used in v. {{Psalm 51:16|16}} does not refer to expiatory sacrifices, but to dedication and communion offerings. This is not a categorical denial of the sacrificial system in general or of the importance of such offerings. The psalmist is talking about his specific situation. Dedication and communion offerings have their proper place in worship (see v. {{Psalm 51:19|19}}), but God requires something more fundamental, a repentant and humble attitude (see v. {{Psalm 51:17|17}}), before these offerings can have real meaning.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “a broken spirit.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “a broken and crushed heart.”

*Translator's note:* Or “despise.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “do what is good for Zion in your favor.”

*Translator's note:* Or “Build.” The imperfect verbal form is used here to express the psalmist’s wish or request.

*Translator's note:* Or “desire, take delight in.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “then they will offer up bulls.” The third plural subject is indefinite.

*Study note:* Verses {{Psalm 51:18|18-19}} appear to reflect the exilic period, when the city’s walls lay in ruins and the sacrificial system had been disrupted.

*Study note:* *Psalm 52*. The psalmist confidently confronts his enemy and affirms that God will destroy evildoers and vindicate the godly.

*Translator's note:* The meaning of the Hebrew term מַשְׂכִּיל (maskil) is uncertain. The word is derived from a verb meaning “to be prudent; to be wise.” Various options are: “a contemplative song,” “a song imparting moral wisdom,” or “a skillful [i.e., well-written] song.” The term occurs in the superscriptions of {{Psalm 32|Pss 32}}, {{Psalm 42|42}}, {{Psalm 44|44}}, {{Psalm 45|45}}, {{Psalm 52|52-55}}, {{Psalm 74|74}}, {{Psalm 78|78}}, {{Psalm 88|88}}, {{Psalm 89|89}}, and {{Psalm 142|142}}, as well as in {{Psalm 47:7|Ps 47:7}}.

*Study note:* According to the superscription, David wrote this psalm during the period when Saul was seeking his life. On one occasion Doeg the Edomite, Saul’s head shepherd ({{1 Samuel 21:7|1 Sam 21:7}}), informed Saul of David’s whereabouts (see {{1 Samuel 21|1 Sam 21-22}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “when Doeg the Edomite came and told Saul and said to him, ‘David has come to the house of Ahimelech.’”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Why do you boast in evil?”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the loyal love of God [is] all the day.” In this context, where the psalmist is threatened by his enemy, the point seems to be that the psalmist is protected by God’s loyal love at all times.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “destruction your tongue devises.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “like a sharpened razor, doer of deceit.” The masculine participle עָשָׂה (ʿasah) is understood as a substantival vocative, addressed to the powerful man.
*Translator's note:* Or “deceit more than speaking what is right.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “you love all the words of swallowing.” Traditionally בַּלַּע (balaʿ) has been taken to mean “swallowing” in the sense of “devouring” or “destructive” (see BDB 118 s.v. בָּלַע). *HALOT* 135 s.v. III *בֶּלַע proposes a homonym here, meaning “confusion.” This would fit the immediate context nicely and provide a close parallel to the following line, which refers to deceptive words.

*Translator's note:* The adverb גַּם (gam, “also; even”) is translated here in an adversative sense (“yet”). It highlights the contrastive correspondence between the evildoer’s behavior and God’s response.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “will tear you down forever.”

*Translator's note:* This rare verb (חָתָה, khatah) occurs only here and in {{Proverbs 6:27|Prov 6:27}}; {{Proverbs 25:22|25:22}}; {{Isaiah 30:14|Isa 30:14}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “from [your] tent.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and the godly will see and will fear and at him will laugh.”

*Translator's note:* The imperfect verbal form here draws attention to the ongoing nature of the action. The evildoer customarily rejected God and trusted in his own abilities. Another option is to take the imperfect as generalizing, “[here is the man who] does not make.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “he was strong in his destruction.” “Destruction” must refer back to the destructive plans mentioned in v. {{Psalm 52:2|2}}. The verb (derived from the root עָזַז, ʿazaz, “be strong”) as it stands is either an imperfect (if so, probably used in a customary sense) or a preterite (without vav [ו] consecutive). However the form should probably be emended to וַיָּעָז (vayyaʿaz), a Qal preterite (with vav [ו] consecutive) from עָזַז. Note the preterite form without vav (ו) consecutive in the preceding line (וַיִּבְטַח, vayyivtakh, “and he trusted”). The prefixed vav (ו) was likely omitted by haplography (note the suffixed vav [ו] on the preceding עָשְׁרוֹ, ʿoshro, “his wealth”).

*Translator's note:* The disjunctive construction (vav [ו] + subject) highlights the contrast between the evildoer’s destiny (vv. {{Psalm 52:5|5-7}}) and that of the godly psalmist’s security.

*Translator's note:* Or “luxuriant, green, leafy.”

*Translator's note:* Or, hyperbolically, “forever and ever.”

*Translator's note:* Or, hyperbolically, “forever.”

*Translator's note:* Or “for.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “you have acted.” The perfect verbal form (1) probably indicates a future perfect here. The psalmist promises to give thanks when the expected vindication has been accomplished. Other options include (2) a generalizing (“for you act”) or (3) rhetorical (“for you will act”) use.

*Translator's note:* Or “wait on.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “your name.” God’s “name” refers here to his reputation and revealed character.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “for it is good in front of your loyal followers.”

*Study note:* *Psalm 53*. This psalm is very similar to Ps 14. The major difference comes in v. 5, which corresponds to, but differs quite a bit from, Ps 14:5-6, and in the use of the divine name. Ps 14 uses “the Lord” (יְהוָה, yehvah, “Yahweh”) in vv. 2a, 4, 6, and 7, while Ps 53 employs “God” (אֱלֹהִים, ’elohim) throughout, as one might expect in Pss 42-83, where the name “Yahweh” is relatively infrequent. The psalmist observes that the human race is morally corrupt. Evildoers oppress God’s people, but the psalmist is confident of God’s protection and anticipates a day when God will vindicate Israel.

*Translator's note:* The meaning of the Hebrew term מָחֲלַת (makhalat, “machalath”) is uncertain; perhaps it refers to a particular style of music, a tune title, or a musical instrument. The term also appears in the heading of {{Psalm 88|Ps 88}}.

*Translator's note:* The meaning of the Hebrew term מַשְׂכִּיל (maskil) is uncertain. See the note on the phrase “well-written song” in the superscription of {{Psalm 52|Ps 52}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “a fool says in his heart.” The singular is used here in a collective or representative sense; the typical fool is envisioned.

*Study note:* *There is no God*. This statement is probably not a philosophical assertion that God does not exist, but rather a confident affirmation that he is unconcerned about how men live morally and ethically (see {{Psalm 10:4|Ps 10:4}}, {{Psalm 10:11|11}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “they act corruptly, they do evil [with] injustice.” {{Psalm 14:1|Ps 14:1}} has עֲלִילָה (ʿalilah, “a deed”) instead of עָוֶל (ʿaval, “injustice”). The verbs describe the typical behavior of the wicked. The subject of the plural verbs is “sons of man” (v. {{Psalm 53:2|2}}). The entire human race is characterized by sinful behavior. This practical atheism—living as if there is no God who will hold them accountable for their actions—makes them fools, for one of the earmarks of folly is to fail to anticipate the long range consequences of one’s behavior.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “there is none that does good.”

*Study note:* The picture of the Lord looking *down from heaven* draws attention to his sovereignty over the world.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “upon the sons of man.”

*Translator's note:* Or “acts wisely.” The Hiphil is exhibitive.

*Translator's note:* That is, who seeks to have a relationship with God by obeying and worshiping him.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “all of it turns away.” {{Psalm 14:1|Ps 14:1}} has הָכֹּל (hakkol, “the whole/all”) instead of כֻּלּוֹ (kullo, “all of it”) and סָר (sar, “turn aside”) instead of סָג (sag, “turn away”).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “together they are corrupt.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “there is none that does good.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the workers of wickedness.” See {{Psalm 5:5|Pss 5:5}}; {{Psalm 6:8|6:8}}. {{Psalm 14:4|Ps 14:4}} adds כֹּל (kol, “all of”) before “workers of wickedness.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Do they not understand?” The rhetorical question expresses the psalmist’s amazement at their apparent lack of understanding. This may refer to their lack of moral understanding, but it more likely refers to their failure to anticipate God’s defense of his people (see vv. {{Psalm 53:5|5-6}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “there they are afraid [with] fear.” The perfect verbal form is probably used in a rhetorical manner; the psalmist describes the future demise of the oppressors as if it were already occurring. The adverb שָׁם (sham, “there”) is also used here for dramatic effect, as the psalmist envisions the wicked standing in fear at a spot that is this vivid in his imagination (BDB 1027 s.v.). The cognate accusative following the verb emphasizes the degree of their terror (“absolutely”).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “there is no fear.” Apparently this means the evildoers are so traumatized with panic (see v. {{Psalm 53:5|5b}}) that they now jump with fear at everything, even those things that would not normally cause fear. {{Psalm 14:5|Ps 14:5}} omits this line.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “scatters the bones.” The perfect is used in a rhetorical manner, describing this future judgment as if it were already accomplished. Scattering the bones alludes to the aftermath of a battle. God annihilates his enemies, leaving their carcasses spread all over the battlefield. As the bodies are devoured by wild animals and decay, the bones of God’s dead enemies are exposed. See {{Psalm 141:7|Ps 141:7}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “[those who] encamp [against] you.” The second person masculine singular pronominal suffix probably refers to God’s people viewed as a collective whole. Instead of “for God scatters the bones of those who encamp against you,” {{Psalm 14:5|Ps 14:5}} reads, “for God is with a godly generation.”

*Translator's note:* Once again the perfect is used in a rhetorical manner, describing this future judgment as if it were already accomplished. As in the previous line, God’s people are probably addressed. The second person singular verb form is apparently collective, suggesting that the people are viewed here as a unified whole. {{Psalm 14:6|Ps 14:6}} reads here “the counsel of the oppressed you put to shame, even though God is his shelter,” the words being addressed to the wicked.

*Translator's note:* This refers metonymically to God, the one who lives in Zion and provides deliverance for Israel.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “turns with a turning [toward] his people.” The Hebrew term שְׁבוּת (shevut) is apparently a cognate accusative of שׁוּב (shuv).

*Translator's note:* The verb form is jussive.

*Translator's note:* Because the parallel verb is jussive, this verb, which is ambiguous in form, should be taken as a jussive as well.

*Study note:* *Psalm 54*. The psalmist asks God for protection against his enemies, confidently affirms that God will vindicate him, and promises to give thanks to God for his saving intervention.

*Translator's note:* The meaning of the Hebrew term מַשְׂכִּיל (maskil) is uncertain. See the note on the phrase “well-written song” in the superscription of {{Psalm 52|Ps 52}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Is not David hiding with us?”

*Study note:* According to the superscription, David wrote this psalm during the period when Saul was seeking his life. On one occasion the Ziphites informed Saul that David was hiding in their territory (see {{1 Samuel 23:19|1 Sam 23:19-20}}).

*Translator's note:* God’s “name” refers here to his reputation and revealed character, which would instill fear in the psalmist’s enemies (see C. A. Briggs and E. G. Briggs, *Psalms* [ICC], 2:17).

*Translator's note:* The imperfect verbal form is used here to express the psalmist’s wish or request.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “to the words of my mouth.”

*Text-critical note:* Many medieval Hebrew mss read זֵדִים (zedim, “proud ones”) rather than זָרִים (zarim, “foreigners”). This is a case of confusing ד (dalet) and ר (resh). The term זֵדִים (zedim) occurs in parallelism with עָרִיצִים (ʿaritsim, “violent ones”) in {{Psalm 86:14|Ps 86:14}} and {{Isaiah 13:11|Isa 13:11}}. However, זָרִים (zarim) is parallel to עָרִיצִים in {{Isaiah 25:5|Isa 25:5}}; {{Isaiah 29:5|29:5}}; {{Ezekiel 28:7|Ezek 28:7}}; {{Ezekiel 31:12|31:12}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “rise against me.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and ruthless ones seek my life, they do not set God in front of them.”

*Translator's note:* Or “my helper.”

*Translator's note:* Or “sustain my life.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “to those who watch me [with evil intent].” See also {{Psalm 5:8|Pss 5:8}}; {{Psalm 27:11|27:11}}; {{Psalm 56:2|56:2}}.

*Translator's note:* The *Kethib* (consonantal text) reads a Qal imperfect, “the evil will return,” while the *Qere* (marginal reading) has a Hiphil imperfect, “he will repay.” The parallel line has an imperative (indicating a prayer/request), so it is best to read a jussive form יָשֹׁב (yashov, “let it [the evil] return”) here.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “in [or “by”] your faithfulness.”
*Translator's note:* The cohortative verbal form expresses the psalmist’s resolve/vow to praise.

*Translator's note:* Or “for,” indicating a more specific reason why he will praise the Lord’s name (cf. v. {{Psalm 54:6|6}}).

*Translator's note:* The perfects in v. {{Psalm 54:7|7}} are probably rhetorical, indicating the psalmist’s certitude and confidence that God will intervene. The psalmist is so confident of God’s positive response to his prayer, he can describe God’s deliverance and his own vindication as if they were occurring or had already occurred.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and on my enemies my eyes look.”

*Study note:* *Psalm 55*. The suffering and oppressed author laments that one of his friends has betrayed him, but he is confident that God will vindicate him by punishing his deceitful enemies.

*Translator's note:* The meaning of the Hebrew term מַשְׂכִּיל (maskil) is uncertain. See the note on the phrase “well-written song” in the superscription of {{Psalm 52|Ps 52}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “hide yourself from.”

*Translator's note:* Or “restless” (see {{Genesis 27:40|Gen 27:40}}). The Hiphil is intransitive-exhibitive, indicating the outward display of an inner attitude.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “in my complaint.”

*Translator's note:* The verb is a Hiphil cohortative from הוּם (hum), which means “to confuse someone” in the Qal and “to go wild” in the Niphal. An Arabic cognate means “to be out of one’s senses, to wander about.” With the vav (ו) conjunctive prefixed to it, the cohortative probably indicates the result or effect of the preceding main verb. Some prefer to emend the form to וְאֵהוֹמָה (veʾehomah), a Niphal of הוּם (hum), or to וְאֶהַמֶה (veʾehameh), a Qal imperfect from הָמָה (hamah, “to moan”). Many also prefer to take this verb with what follows (see v. {{Psalm 55:3|3}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “because of [the] voice of [the] enemy.”

*Translator's note:* The singular forms “enemy” and “wicked” are collective or representative, as the plural verb forms in the second half of the verse indicate.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “from before the pressure of the wicked.” Some suggest the meaning “screech” (note the parallel “voice”; cf. NEB “shrill clamour”; NRSV “clamor”) for the rare noun עָקָה (ʿaqah, “pressure”).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “wickedness,” but here the term refers to the destructive effects of their wicked acts.

*Text-critical note:* The meaning of the MT is unclear. The *Kethib* (consonantal text) reads יַשִּׁימָוֶת עָלֵימוֹ (yashimavet ʿalemo, “May devastation [be] upon them.”). The proposed noun יַשִּׁימָוֶת occurs only here and perhaps in the place name Beth Jeshimoth in {{Numbers 33:49|Num 33:49}}. The *Qere* (marginal text) has יַשִּׁי מָוֶת עָלֵימוֹ (yashi mavet ʿalemo). The verbal form יַשִּׁי is apparently an alternate form of יַשִּׁיא (yashiʾ), a Hiphil imperfect from נָשַׁא (nashaʾ, “deceive”). In this case one might read “death will come deceptively upon them.” This reading has the advantage of reading מָוֶת (mavet, “death”) which forms a natural parallel with “Sheol” in the next line. The present translation is based on the following reconstruction of the text: יְשִׁמֵּם מָוֶת (yeshimmem mavet). The verb assumed in the reconstruction is a Hiphil jussive third masculine singular from שָׁמַם (shamam, “be desolate”) with a third masculine plural pronominal suffix attached. This reconstruction assumes that (1) haplography has occurred in the traditional text (the original sequence of three mems [מ] was lost with only one mem remaining), resulting in the fusion of originally distinct forms in the *Kethib*, and (2) that עָלֵימוֹ (ʿalemo, “upon them”) is a later scribal addition attempting to make sense of a garbled text. The preposition עַל (ʿal) does occur with the verb שָׁמַם (shamam), but in such cases the expression means “be appalled at/because of” (see Jer 49:20; 50:45). If one were to retain the prepositional phrase here, one would have to read the text as follows: יַשִּׁים מָוֶת עָלֵימוֹ (yashim mavet ʿalemo, “Death will be appalled at them”). The idea seems odd, to say the least. Death is not collocated with this verb elsewhere.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “in God I boast, his word.” The syntax in the Hebrew text is difficult. God’s “word” is here understood as an assuring promise of protection. Another option (2) is to translate, “in God I will boast [with] a word.” In this case, the “word” is a song of praise. (In this view the pronominal suffix “his” must be omitted as in v. {{Psalm 56:10|10}}.) The present translation reflects yet another option (3): In this case “I praise his word” is a parenthetical statement, with “his word” being the object of the verb. The present translation assumes an emendation to אֵלִם (ʾelim), which in turn is understood as a defectively written form of אֵילִים (ʾelim, “rulers,” a metaphorical use of אַיִל, ʾayil, “ram”; see {{Exodus 15:15|Exod 15:15}}; {{Ezekiel 17:13|Ezek 17:13}}). The rhetorical question is sarcastic, challenging their claim to be just. Elsewhere the collocation of דָּבַר (davar, “speak”) with צֶדֶק (tsedeq, “what is right”) as object means “to speak the truth” (see {{Psalm 52:3|Ps 52:3}}; {{Isaiah 45:19|Isa 45:19}}). Here it refers specifically to declaring what is right in a legal setting, as the next line indicates.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the sons of mankind.” The translation assumes the phrase is the object of the verb “to judge.” Some take it as a vocative, “Do you judge fairly, O sons of mankind?” (Cf. NASB; see {{Ezekiel 20:4|Ezek 20:4}}; {{Ezekiel 22:2|22:2}}; {{Ezekiel 23:36|23:36}}.)

*Translator's note:* The particle אַף (ʾaf, “no”) is used here as a strong adversative emphasizing the following statement, which contrasts reality with the rulers’ claim alluded to in the rhetorical questions (see {{Psalm 44:9|Ps 44:9}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “in the heart unjust deeds you do.” The phrase “in the heart” (i.e., “mind”) seems to refer to their plans and motives. The Hebrew noun עַוְלָה (ʿavlah, “injustice”) is collocated with פָּעַל (paʿal, “do”) here and in {{Job 36:23|Job 36:23}} and {{Psalm 119:3|Ps 119:3}}. Some emend the plural form עוֹלֹת (ʿolot, “unjust deeds”; see {{Psalm 64:6|Ps 64:6}}) to the singular עָוֶל (ʿavel, “injustice”; see {{Job 34:32|Job 34:32}}), taking the final tav (ת) as dittographic (note that the following verbal form begins with *tav*). Some then understand עָוֶל (ʿavel, “injustice”) as a genitive modifying “heart” and translate, “with a heart of injustice you act.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “in the earth the violence of your hands you weigh out.” The imagery is from the economic realm. The addressees measure out violence, rather than justice, and distribute it like a commodity. This may be ironic, since justice was sometimes viewed as a measuring scale (see {{Job 31:6|Job 31:6}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “from the womb.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “speakers of a lie go astray from the womb.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “[there is] venom to them according to the likeness of venom of a snake.”

*Translator's note:* Or perhaps “cobra” (cf. NASB, NIV). Other suggested species of snakes are “asp” (NEB) and “adder” (NRSV).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “[that] stops up its ear.” The apparent Hiphil jussive verbal form should be understood as a Qal imperfect with “i” theme vowel (see GKC 168 §63.*n*).
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “does not listen to the voice of.”

*Translator's note:* Following the imperatival forms in v. {{Psalm 58:6|6}}, the prefixed verbal form is understood as a jussive expressing the psalmist’s wish. Another option is to take the form as an imperfect (indicative) and translate, “they will scatter” (see v. {{Psalm 58:9|9}}). The verb מָאַס (maʾas; which is a homonym of the more common מָאַס, “to refuse, reject”) appears only here and in {{Job 7:5|Job 7:5}}, where it is used of a festering wound from which fluid runs or flows.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “like water, they go about for themselves.” The translation assumes that the phrase “they go about for themselves” is an implied relative clause modifying “water.” Another option is to take the clause as independent and parallel to what precedes. In this case the enemies would be the subject and the verb could be taken as jussive, “let them wander about.”

*Text-critical note:* The syntax of the Hebrew text is difficult and the meaning uncertain. The text reads literally, “he treads his arrows (following the *Qere*; *Kethib* has “his arrow”), like they are cut off/dry up.” It is not clear if the verbal root is מָלַל (malal, “circumcise”; BDB 576 s.v. IV מָלַל) or the homonym מָלַל (“wither”; *HALOT* 593-94 s.v. I מלל). Since the verb מָלַל (“to wither”) is used of vegetation, it is possible that the noun חָצִיר (khatsir, “grass,” which is visually similar to חִצָּיו, khitsayv, “his arrows”) originally appeared in the text. The translation above assumes that the text originally was כְּמוֹ חָצִיר יִתְמֹלָלוּ (kemo khatsir yitmolalu, “like grass let them wither”). If original, it could have been accidentally changed to חִצָּיו כְּמוֹ יִתְמֹלָלוּ (khitsayv kemo yitmolalu, “his arrow(s) like they dry up”) with דָּרַךְ (darakh, “to tread”) being added later in an effort to make sense of “his arrow(s).”

*Translator's note:* There is no “to be” verb in the Hebrew text at this point, but a jussive tone can be assumed based on vv. {{Psalm 58:6|6-7}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “like a melting snail [that] moves along.” A. Cohen (*Psalms* [SoBB], 184) explains that the text here alludes “to the popular belief that the slimy trail which the snail leaves in its track is the dissolution of its substance.”

*Translator's note:* The words “let them be like” are supplied in the translation for stylistic reasons. The jussive mood is implied from the preceding context, and “like” is understood by ellipsis (see the previous line).

*Translator's note:* This rare word also appears in {{Job 3:16|Job 3:16}} and Eccles 6:3.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “before your pots perceive thorns.”

*Translator's note:* Apparently God (v. {{Psalm 58:6|6}}) is the subject of the verb here.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “like living, like burning anger he will sweep it away.” The meaning of the text is unclear. The translation assumes that within the cooking metaphor (see the previous line) חַי (khay, “living”) refers here to raw meat (as in {{1 Samuel 2:15|1 Sam 2:15}}, where it modifies בָּשָׂר, basar, “flesh”) and that חָרוּן (kharun; which always refers to God’s “burning anger” elsewhere) here refers to food that is cooked. The pronominal suffix on the verb “sweep away” apparently refers back to the “thorns” of the preceding line. The image depicts swift and sudden judgment. Before the fire has been adequately kindled and all the meat cooked, the winds of judgment will sweep away everything in their path.
*Translator's note:* The singular is representative here, as is the singular from “wicked” in the next line.

*Translator's note:* Following the imperfects of v. {{Psalm 58:10|10}}, the prefixed verbal form with vav (ו) conjunctive probably indicates a result or consequence of what precedes.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “man.” The singular is representative here.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “surely [there] is fruit for the godly.”

*Translator's note:* The plural participle is unusual here if the preceding אֱלֹהִים (ʾelohim) is here a plural of majesty, referring to the one true God. Occasionally the plural of majesty does take a plural attributive (see GKC 428-29 §132.*h*). It is possible that the final mem (ם) on the participle is enclitic, and that it was later misunderstood as a plural ending. Another option is to translate, “Yes indeed, there are gods who judge in the earth.” In this case, the statement reflects the polytheistic mindset of pagan observers who, despite their theological ignorance, nevertheless recognize divine retribution when they see it.

*Study note:* *Psalm 59*. The psalmist calls down judgment on his foreign enemies, whom he compares to ravenous wild dogs.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “do not destroy.” Perhaps this refers to a particular style of music, a tune title, or a musical instrument. These words also appear in the superscription to {{Psalm 57|Pss 57-58}}, {{Psalm 75|75}}.

*Translator's note:* The precise meaning of the Hebrew word מִכְתָּם (miktam), which also appears in the heading to {{Psalm 16|Pss 16}}, {{Psalm 56|56-58}}, {{Psalm 60|60}} is uncertain. *HALOT* 582-83 s.v. defines it as “inscription.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “when Saul sent and they watched his house in order to kill him.”

*Study note:* According to the superscription, David wrote this psalm on the occasion when Saul sent assassins to surround David’s house and kill him in the morning (see {{1 Samuel 19:11|1 Sam 19:11}}). However, the psalm itself mentions foreign enemies (vv. {{Psalm 59:5|5}}, {{Psalm 59:8|8}}). Perhaps these references reflect a later adaptation of an original Davidic psalm.

*Translator's note:* Or “make me secure”; *Heb* “set me on high.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “from those who raise themselves up [against] me.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “from the workers of wickedness.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “from men of bloodshed.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “my life.”

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew verb is from the root גּוּר (gur), which means “to challenge, attack” in {{Isaiah 54:15|Isa 54:15}} and “to stalk” (with hostile intent) in {{Psalm 56:8|Ps 56:8}}.

*Study note:* The point is that the psalmist’s enemies have no justifiable reason for attacking him. He has neither *rebelled or sinned* against the Lord.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “without sin.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “they run and they are determined.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “arise to meet me and see.” The Hebrew verb קָרָא (qaraʾ, “to meet; to encounter”) here carries the nuance of “to help.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Lord, God, Hosts.” One expects the construct form אֱלֹהֵי (ʾelohe) before צְבָאוֹת (tsevaʾot, “hosts”). See {{Psalm 89:9|Ps 89:9}}, but יְהוָה אֱלֹהִים (yehvah ʾelohim) precedes צְבָאוֹת (tsevaʾot) in {{Psalm 80:4|Pss 80:4}}, {{Psalm 80:19|19}}; {{Psalm 84:8|84:8}} as well.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “wake up to punish” (see {{Psalm 35:23|Pss 35:23}}; {{Psalm 44:23|44:23}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “look, they gush forth with their mouth, swords [are] in their lips.”

*Translator's note:* The words “for they say” are supplied in the translation for clarification. The following question (“Who hears?”) is spoken by the psalmist’s enemies, who are confident that no one else can hear their threats against the psalmist. They are aggressive because they feel the psalmist is vulnerable and has no one to help him.

*Study note:* *Laugh in disgust*. See {{Psalm 2:4|Pss 2:4}}; {{Psalm 37:13|37:13}}.

*Translator's note:* Or “scoff at”; or “deride”; or “mock” (see {{Psalm 2:4|Ps 2:4}}).

*Text-critical note:* *Heb* “his strength, for you I will watch.” “His strength” should be emended to “my strength” (see v. {{Psalm 59:17|17}}). Some also emend אֶשְׁמֹרָה (ʾeshmorah, “I will watch”) to אֱזַמֵּרָה (ʾezammerah, “I will sing praises [to you]”) See v. {{Psalm 59:17|17}}.

*Translator's note:* Or “my elevated place” (see {{Psalm 18:2|Ps 18:2}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the God of my [*Qere* (marginal reading); the *Kethib* (consonantal text) has “his”] loyal love will meet me.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “will cause me to look upon.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “those who watch me [with evil intent].” See also {{Psalm 5:8|Pss 5:8}}; {{Psalm 27:11|27:11}}; {{Psalm 54:5|54:5}}; {{Psalm 56:2|56:2}}.

*Study note:* *My people might forget the lesson*. Swift, sudden destruction might be quickly forgotten. The psalmist wants God’s judgment to be prolonged so that it might be a continual reminder of divine justice.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “do not kill them, lest my people forget.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “make them roam around by your strength and bring them down, O our shield, the Lord.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the sin of their mouth [is] the word of their lips.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “if they are not full, they stay through the night.”

*Translator's note:* Or “my elevated place” (see {{Psalm 18:2|Ps 18:2}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and my shelter in the day of my distress.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “my strength, to you I will sing praises.”

*Translator's note:* Or “my elevated place” (see {{Psalm 18:2|Ps 18:2}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the God of my loyal love.”

*Study note:* *Psalm 60*. The psalmist grieves over Israel’s humiliation, but in response to God’s assuring word, he asks for divine help in battle and expresses his confidence in victory.

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew expression means “lily of the testimony.” It may refer to a particular music style or to a tune title.

*Translator's note:* The precise meaning of the Hebrew word מִכְתָּם (miktam), which also appears in the heading to {{Psalm 16|Pss 16}}, {{Psalm 56|56-59}}, is uncertain. *HALOT* 582-83 s.v. defines it as “inscription.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “to teach.”

*Translator's note:* In {{Joshua 8:21|Josh 8:21}} and {{Judges 20:48|Judg 20:48}} the two verbs “turn back” and “strike down” are also juxtaposed. There they refer to a military counter-attack.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “12,000 of Edom.” Perhaps one should read אֲרַם (’aram, “Aram”) here rather than אֱדוֹם (’edom, “Edom”).

*Study note:* The heading apparently refers to the military campaign recorded in {{2 Samuel 10|2 Sam 10}} and 1 Chr 19.

*Study note:* *You have rejected us*. See {{Psalm 43:2|Pss 43:2}}; {{Psalm 44:9|44:9}}, {{Psalm 44:23|23}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “you broke out upon us, you were angry.”

*Translator's note:* The imperfect verbal form here expresses the psalmist’s wish or prayer.

*Translator's note:* The verb פָּצַם (patsam, “split open”) occurs only here in the OT. An Arabic cognate means “crack,” and an Aramaic cognate is used in *Tg*. Jer 22:14 with the meaning “break open, frame.” See BDB 822 s.v. and Jastrow 1205 s.v. פְּצַם.

*Study note:* *You made the earth quake; you split it open*. The psalmist uses the imagery of an earthquake to describe the nation’s defeat.

*Study note:* *It is ready to fall*. The earth is compared to a wall that has been broken by the force of the earthquake (note the preceding line) and is ready to collapse.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “you have caused your people to see [what is] hard.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “wine of staggering,” that is, intoxicating wine that makes one stagger in drunkenness. Intoxicating wine is here an image of divine judgment that makes its victims stagger like drunkards. See {{Isaiah 51:17|Isa 51:17-23}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “those who fear you.”

*Translator's note:* There is a ray of hope in that God has allowed his loyal followers to rally under a battle flag. The translation assumes the verb is from the root נוּס (nus, “flee”) used here in the Hitpolel in the sense of “find safety for oneself” (*HALOT* 681 s.v. נוס) or “take flight for oneself” (BDB 630-31 s.v. נוּס). Another option is to take the verb as a denominative from נֵס (nes, “flag”) and translate “that it may be displayed” (BDB 651 s.v. II נסס) or “that they may assemble under the banner” (*HALOT* 704 s.v. II נסס). Here קֹשֶׁט (qoshet) is taken as an Aramaized form of קֶשֶׁת (qeshet, “bow”; BDB 905-6 s.v. קֶשֶׁת), though some understand the homonymic קֹשְׁטְ (qoshet, “truth”) here (see {{Proverbs 22:21|Prov 22:21}}; cf. NASB). If one follows the latter interpretation, the line may be translated, “so that they might assemble under the banner for the sake of truth.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “right hand.”

*Translator's note:* The *Qere* (marginal reading) has “me,” while the *Kethib* (consonantal text) has “us.”

*Translator's note:* Or “may be rescued.” The lines are actually reversed in the Hebrew text, “So that the ones you love may be rescued, deliver by your power and answer me.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “in his holy place.”

*Study note:* *Shechem* stands for the territory west of the Jordan, the *Valley of Sukkoth* for the region east of the Jordan.

*Study note:* *Gilead* was located east of the Jordan. Half of the tribe of *Manasseh* lived east of the Jordan in the region of Bashan.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the protection of my head.”

*Study note:* *Ephraim*, named after one of Joseph’s sons, was one of two major tribes located west of the Jordan. By comparing Ephraim to a helmet, the Lord suggests that the Ephraimites played a primary role in the defense of his land.

*Study note:* *Judah*, like Ephraim, was the other major tribe west of the Jordan. The Davidic king, symbolized here by the *royal scepter*, came from this tribe.

*Study note:* The metaphor of the *washbasin*, used to rinse one’s hands and feet, suggests that *Moab*, in contrast to Israel’s elevated position (vv. {{Psalm 60:6|6-7}}), would be reduced to the status of a servant.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “over Edom I will throw my sandal.” The point of the metaphor is not entirely clear. Some interpret this as idiomatic for “taking possession of,” i.e., “I will take possession of Edom.” Others translate עַל (ʿal) as “to” and understand this as referring to a master throwing his dirty sandal to a servant so that the latter might dust it off.

*Text-critical note:* *Heb* “over me, O Philistia, shout in triumph.” The translation follows the text of {{Psalm 108:9|Ps 108:9}}. When the initial עֲלֵיוֹ (ʿaleyo, “over”) was misread as עָלַי (ʿalay, “over me”), the first person verb form was probably altered to an imperative to provide better sense to the line.

*Study note:* In v. {{Psalm 60:9|9}} the psalmist speaks again and acknowledges his need for help in battle. He hopes God will volunteer, based on the affirmation of sovereignty over Edom in v. {{Psalm 60:8|8}}, but he is also aware that God has seemingly rejected the nation (v. {{Psalm 60:10|10}}, see also v. {{Psalm 60:1|1}}).
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and futile [is] the deliverance of man.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “in God we will accomplish strength.” The statement refers here to military success (see {{Numbers 24:18|Num 24:18}}; {{1 Samuel 14:48|1 Sam 14:48}}; {{Psalm 108:13|Pss 108:13}}; {{Psalm 118:15|118:15-16}}).

*Study note:* *Trample down*. On this expression see {{Psalm 44:5|Ps 44:5}}.
